planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in fall so roots establish before summer drought; leather oak demands lean, rocky, magnesium-heavy serpentine-type soil and resents amended garden beds with normal fertility.

directions: This slow-growing, holly-leaved evergreen shrub forms dense thickets on the thin, rocky, nutrient-poor serpentine barrens of the California Coast Ranges, where few other shrubs can compete. The small, cupped, spine-toothed leaves reduce water loss and give the plant a tough, leathery texture that discourages browsing. It needs sharp drainage and essentially no summer water once established, making it a fitting anchor for a dry serpentine-themed rock garden rather than a conventional shrub border. Because it tolerates serpentine's unusual mineral balance, it is often paired with other barren specialists in restoration plantings on degraded rangeland.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall onto lean, unamended, sharply drained soil; seedlings overwinter as small basal rosettes and bloom in their second summer, needing no irrigation once the taproot is established.

directions: Golden buckwheat grows as a low, woolly-leaved subshrub across dry, open serpentine and other poor-soil barrens in central and northern California, sending up branched stems topped with small cream-to-pale-yellow flower clusters that age to rust through late summer. Its wiry, long-blooming flowerheads are a reliable late-season nectar source for small native bees and butterflies when most other barrens wildflowers have gone to seed. The tight basal mat of gray-green leaves helps it hold a foothold in gravelly, infertile ground where competing grasses struggle. It suits a gravel garden or dryland rock planting where its understated color and persistent dried flowerheads carry interest into fall.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall into rocky, fast-draining soil under dappled high shade; the species needs a dry summer rest and will rot if watered after foliage yellows.

directions: A diminutive mariposa-lily relative, this star-tulip grows in the thin duff and rocky openings at the edge of serpentine chaparral and oak woodland in the East Bay hills, where it catches filtered light before overhead canopy closes in. Each slender stem carries a nodding cluster of small white-to-pale-lavender, star-shaped flowers with a sparse fringe of hairs inside, opening in early spring while soil is still moist from winter rain. It disappears completely below ground through the dry summer, re-emerging only after fall rains return, so it pairs well with other dry-dormant bulbs rather than thirsty perennial companions. Grow it in a raised rock bed or bulb frame where its tiny scale will not be lost among larger plants.

planting.note: Transplant from containers in fall into lean, rocky, unamended soil with excellent drainage; established plants need no summer water and decline quickly if kept moist.

directions: Endemic to the serpentine and sandstone outcrops of the Santa Lucia and San Luis Obispo ranges, this manzanita forms a rounded, many-branched evergreen shrub with the smooth mahogany bark typical of the genus. Small, urn-shaped white-to-pink flower clusters open in winter and draw early-season native bees and hummingbirds before most other chaparral shrubs have broken dormancy. Its tough, rounded leaves and wiry structure let it persist on exposed, thin-soiled barrens that bake in summer and stay cool and damp through winter fog. It works best as a specimen or background shrub in a dry chaparral-style planting, kept well away from summer-irrigated beds or lawn runoff that can trigger root rot.

planting.note: Set out young container trees in fall on lean, rocky, often serpentine-derived soil with full sun exposure; avoid rich garden loam, summer irrigation, and low-lying frost pockets.

directions: MacNab cypress is a small, shrubby conifer scattered across scalded serpentine and other mineral-poor barrens in the northern California Coast Ranges, where it survives conditions too harsh for most competing trees. Its foliage has a distinctive resinous, almost pungent scent when crushed, and mature trees carry small, knobby cones that can persist closed on the branches for years before releasing seed, often triggered by fire. Growth is naturally gnarled and open rather than the tidy pyramidal form of landscape cypress cultivars, giving it a bonsai-like character valued by conifer collectors and serpentine-habitat restoration plantings alike. It needs full sun and lean soil to stay healthy, declining in shaded or over-watered garden settings.

planting.note: Plant young trees in fall into unamended, rocky serpentine-type soil in full sun; the species is adapted to periodic fire and performs poorly in irrigated, fertile landscape beds.

directions: Sargent cypress is almost entirely restricted to serpentine outcrops scattered through the California Coast Ranges, forming open, scrubby woodlands or, on the thinnest soils, stunted dwarf stands only a few feet tall. Where soil pockets are deeper it can grow into a narrow, pyramidal tree, but its growth form tracks the underlying rock so closely that stand height is often used as a rough map of serpentine soil depth. Its small, gray-brown cones are serotinous, staying sealed on the tree for years and opening en masse after fire passes through, which regenerates whole stands at once. Collectors and restoration growers value it for exactly the toughness that makes it unsuitable for ordinary irrigated gardens; it belongs in a dry, rocky, fire-adapted planting rather than a conventional yard.

planting.note: Divide or transplant rooted sections in fall onto lean, rocky, fast-draining banks in full sun; this rhizomatous native spreads slowly and needs no summer irrigation once rooted.

directions: This low, trailing native morning glory threads through gravelly openings in serpentine chaparral and grassland in the North and Central Coast Ranges, holding dry, erosion-prone banks with a spreading rhizome rather than climbing like its weedy bindweed relatives. Funnel-shaped flowers in white to soft pink open through spring and into early summer against gray-green, arrow-shaped leaves, giving a tidy, non-aggressive ground cover for a dry bank where little else will take hold. Because it is a true native rhizome and not the invasive field bindweed it superficially resembles, it is sometimes chosen specifically to displace that weed on serpentine restoration sites. It wants lean, mineral soil and full sun, going dormant and dying back cleanly through the driest months.
